content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper considers using deep learning to speed up solving PDEs. They build a new iterator on top of existing standard hand-crafted iterative solvers. The current iterative result is modified by a deep convolutional network to achieve faster convergence.  The unfixed bias iterator is introduced to provide sufficient theoretical guarantees. Finally, they show sufficient numerical experiments their iterator has a convergence speed far beyond that of other iterators and exhibits strong generalization ability.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength: This paper proposes a new unified bias iterator to improve both theoretical and experimental guarantees for the deep learning to PDEs.

Weaknesses: The numerical experiments still need to be strengthened.The theory is not enough to support their experiments
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is presented clearly.  However, the novelty and reproducibility looks not enough.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposes an improvement in using deep learning to accelerate numerically solving PDE, but the novelty is limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This work proposes a momentum approach to accelerate the convergence of existing neural-net-based PDE solvers. 
In particular, it builds on existing PDE solvers and uses a deep convolutional network to modify the current result, while relying on past history of iterative results.
The difference with previous works is that at each iteration the past two residuals are used to make a correction at the current step.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
I think that the overall idea of using momentum type of updates for PDE solvers is very interesting. I do think that this is a promising direction. However, it would be relevant to provide more rigorous convergence analyses for some setups, as well as to further explore this idea with different momentum types so as to make the message conclusive. 


### Minor: 
- in the abstract, instead of *exhibits strong generalization ability*, use simply *generalizes well*.
- please use *\citep* for the citations to have parentheses where appropriate; it is hard to read the sentences when these blend with the text
- replace *degenerates* under eq. (3) with *becomes* or *is equivalent to*
- when $T$ and $c_i$ are introduced under eq. (6) specify their dimension(s) 
- make the title more specific to include PDEs
- typo in conclusion *ion*
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Writing/Clarity**. I found that the writing is often informal, for example: *an iterator has generalization* (very imprecise), *[...] the update is not real-time enough*, etc.

**Novelty**. The main novelty of this paper is that it applies an existing momentum method to the method provided Hsieh et al, and the presented theoretical results are incremental relative to the ones in the previous works. Hence, the novelty is limited. 
See also the comment below on Thm. 3.2.

**Citations**. Seems to me that Theorem 3.2. follows trivially from [Bertsekas, 1999], see Proposition 4.4.1 therein. Be specific with the citation for the momentum method, instead of citing an overview paper. 


*Dimitri P Bertsekas. Nonlinear programming. Athena scientific Belmont, 1999.*
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall, I think there is a huge potential in understanding the optimization differences for  PDE solvers, so the general idea is very interesting. However, since this work focuses on exploring momentum on a high output level, the novelty is limited despite that there are some relevant questions that immediately arise (which in turn would make the message more conclusive). For example, addressing some of these: more rigorous convergence analysis for specific problem classes, understanding in which cases does momentum not help (note that in optimization momentum is not optimal for all problem classes), exploring and comparing different types of momentum and not only the one presented, adaptive hyperparameters, etc. Hence, I do not think that this project is ready for publication yet. 

Furthermore, I find that the writing and presentation can be significantly improved (see my comments above). 
In addition, the paper could be improved in terms of citing the relevant works, and better positioning with respect to what is novel, why this change requires significant changes in the theoretical analyses, etc.

content.summary_of_the_paper: In this paper, an unfixed bias iterator is designed to solve partial differential equations. Inspired by the momentum gradient descent method, the iterator modifies the current iterative result by using the residual generated by all adjacent iterations. And they provide sufficient theoretical guarantees for convergence as well as generalization.
content.strength_and_weaknesses: This paper is theoretically sound in general
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and easy to follow with clear comparison to the literature.  Very clear, only minor flaws.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Although this paper is theoretically sound in general, there are still some questions need to be discussed:
1.	There are a lot of document stacks in Introduction. Can you classify them so that readers can better understand how to use deep learning to solve PDEs?
2.	The statement of “inspired by the great success of momentum gradient descent”. Is there a more detailed intuition to explain the relationship between momentum gradient method and unfixed bias iterator?
3.	Theorem 3.2 implies whether the iterator converges depends on T and c. How to ensure that the learned T and c meet such conditions? 
4.	How to ensure that the learned H meets lim HW_n=0  in Theorem 3.3?
5.	The statement “The iterator will simply fail to converge” in the last paragraph in “3.3.3 GENERALIZATION”. What does it mean?
6.	In hand-crafted iterative solvers, the number of iterations  l  can affect accuracy, but in Appendix B, the statement "no objective change in the conversion speed…" is mentioned. What is the reason for this phenomenon?
7.	It says that “obtains SOTA performance…”, but the compared iterators only include the literature Hsieh et al. (2019), can you compare more recent iterators or algorithms?
8.	There are “If  ||a_*||>||a_i||  for all i>=N1  ” in (29) in Lemma A.2, is this an assumption? In other words, how to guarantee such a condition?
9.	Some mistakes
(1)	The 6-th line in “5 CONCLUSION”, “ion” should be “on”
(2)	The statement “According to Theorem 3.2, if our…” in “4.2.1 POSSION EQUATION”, may be “Theorem 3.4”?
(3)	“Let  \varepsilon ” in Lemma A.2, may be “\varepsilon>0 ”?
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
